back: With the system left on, the wheels hang at full droop and the control module reads this as very low ride height. The compressor then tries to fill the fully extended air bags, which can overextend and damage them.

front: What must be done after replacing an air suspension height sensor or its linkage?
back: Most systems require a height calibration using a scan tool so the module learns the new sensor reference points. Since this changes ride height, a wheel alignment check should follow as well.

front: What is a ladder frame and where is it commonly used?
back: A ladder frame is built from two full length steel rails joined by crossmembers, with the body bolted on top through rubber mounts. It is strong and simple, and it is the standard structure on pickup trucks and many truck based SUVs.

front: What is a perimeter frame and how does it differ from a ladder frame?
back: A perimeter frame routes its rails outward around the passenger compartment instead of running straight underneath it. This gives a lower floor and better side impact protection, and it was common on older full size cars.

front: What is unibody (unitized) construction?
back: There is no separate bolt on frame. Stamped panels, rails, and pillars are welded together into a single structure, so the body itself carries all of the vehicle's loads. Nearly all modern cars and crossovers are built this way.

front: What is a subframe (cradle) on a unibody vehicle?
back: It is a bolted in structure under the engine that supports the powertrain, the lower control arms, and often the steering rack. It is a separate piece bolted to the unibody rather than part of the welded structure.

front: A unibody vehicle has alignment readings that are strangely offset from one side to the other on the front axle. What should the technician check?
back: A shifted subframe should be checked, since it changes alignment angles on both front wheels at the same time. Subframe position should always be verified whenever front alignment numbers look mismatched side to side.

front: What is the datum line (datum plane) used in frame measurement?
back: It is an imaginary horizontal plane below the vehicle that vertical heights to specific control points are measured from. It comes from the manufacturer's dimension chart and gives a consistent reference for every measurement.

front: What is the centerline in frame and underbody measurement?
back: It is an imaginary line running lengthwise through the exact centre of the vehicle. Width measurements from this line to control points on each side should be equal if the underbody structure is straight and undamaged.

front: What is X-checking (cross measuring) a frame or unibody?
back: It means measuring diagonally from a control point on one side to the mirror image point on the opposite side, then measuring the opposite diagonal. Equal diagonals within about 3 mm mean that section is square, while a larger difference means damage.

front: What tool lets a technician take point to point frame measurements when parts block a straight tape path?
back: A tram gauge with adjustable pointers can reach around obstructions and still take an accurate point to point measurement. This makes it useful for checking control points that a tape measure cannot reach in a straight line.

front: What is diamond damage on a frame?
back: Diamond damage happens when one frame rail is pushed rearward relative to the other, turning the frame's rectangle shape into a parallelogram. It shows up as unequal X-check diagonals and is usually caused by a hard corner impact.

front: What is sag damage on a frame?
back: Sag means a rail has bowed downward, usually in the section between the wheels. It is caused by a collision or by chronic overloading, and it shows up as a low datum height reading at the affected point.

front: What is sway (sidesway) damage on a frame?
back: Sway means the frame has bent sideways so the front or rear section no longer tracks along the centerline. It is typically caused by a side impact, and the vehicle will dog-track down the road as a result.

front: What is twist damage on a frame?
back: Twist means one rail rides higher than the other, so the frame is no longer flat across its width. The vehicle leans to one side and datum height readings disagree when compared diagonally.

front: What is mash (collapse) damage on a frame?
back: Mash means a section of rail has been shortened by a frontal or rear impact. Length measurements between control points come up short, and visible buckles usually appear in the rail at the damaged section.

front: Why does real collision damage often show more than one of the five classic frame damage types at once?
back: A hard enough impact can push, bend, and shorten the structure in more than one way at the same time. This is why a technician should measure the whole structure with the dimension chart rather than assuming only the obviously damaged area is affected.

front: Control point measurements on a vehicle come back out of specification. What is the correct next step?
back: The vehicle must go to a collision repair facility with a frame straightening system before any alignment is attempted. No amount of alignment adjustment can correct a bent frame or unibody structure.

front: What is ride height (curb height or trim height)?
back: It is the manufacturer's specified distance from defined chassis points to the ground, or between certain suspension points, measured on a level surface. It is measured at curb weight, meaning full fuel, correct tire pressures, and no passengers or cargo, unless the spec says otherwise.

front: How much side to side difference in ride height do most manufacturers allow?
back: Most manufacturers allow only a small side to side difference, commonly in the range of about 10 to 15 mm. Anything beyond that range signals a problem such as a weak spring or sagging suspension on one corner.

front: Why is ride height checked before every wheel alignment?
back: Suspension geometry is designed around the correct ride height, so a sagging vehicle has camber, caster, and toe values shifted away from their designed targets. Aligning a vehicle before fixing ride height only hides the symptom on the machine's readout, not in the actual geometry.

front: A vehicle has correct alignment readings on the machine but the customer still complains of tire wear or poor handling. What is a likely cause the exam expects?
back: Low ride height is a frequent intended answer in this scenario. The alignment numbers can look fine at rest while the suspension geometry through jounce and rebound remains wrong because ride height was never corrected first.

front: What is the correct service sequence when a vehicle has both low ride height and worn alignment angles?
back: First measure ride height, then replace weak springs or adjust torsion bars as needed to bring height back to specification. Only after ride height is corrected should the vehicle be aligned.

front: A vibration changes with vehicle speed but not with engine speed. What does that point to?
back: This points to the wheels, tires, hubs, or brakes rather than the powertrain. Since the vibration tracks road speed instead of engine RPM, an out of balance wheel and tire assembly is a common cause.

front: At what speed range does wheel and tire imbalance typically become noticeable, and how is front versus rear imbalance felt?
back: It typically shows up between about 80 and 110 km/h. A front imbalance is usually felt in the steering wheel, while a rear imbalance is usually felt in the seat instead.

front: A vibration is tied directly to engine speed rather than road speed. What does this suggest?
back: This points to the powertrain mounts or an accessory rather than the suspension or tires. Because the vibration changes with RPM instead of vehicle speed, the suspension system can largely be ruled out.

front: A shake is felt only while braking and disappears otherwise. What does this suggest?
back: This points to brake rotor thickness variation rather than a suspension component. Since the shake only occurs during the braking event itself, the suspension can generally be ruled out as the cause.

front: What does a clunk noise over bumps usually suggest?
back: A clunk over bumps suggests worn stabilizer links, worn control arm bushings, or a loose strut mount. All three allow small amounts of unwanted movement that produce an audible knock when the suspension compresses or rebounds.

front: What does a creak or groan during slow turns or while rocking the vehicle suggest?
back: This suggests dry or worn ball joints. The lack of lubrication or excessive wear in the joint causes friction that produces the creaking or groaning sound during slow steering movement.

front: What does a snap or pop while turning at low speed suggest?
back: This suggests a worn upper strut mount bearing, or on a front wheel drive vehicle it can suggest a worn outer CV joint. Both involve a component that binds and then releases suddenly as the wheel turns.

front: What does a single clunk when shifting between drive and reverse suggest?
back: This suggests worn control arm bushings or worn engine cradle mounts that let components shift slightly under the sudden change in torque direction. The clunk happens once at the moment of the shift rather than continuously.

front: Why should a technician always confirm a suspected worn part before replacing it during noise diagnosis?
back: Noise diagnosis by guesswork often replaces good parts while leaving the actual cause untouched, so the customer's complaint remains unresolved. A physical inspection, pry bar check, or dial indicator measurement should always confirm the suspected part first.

front: What is sprung weight?
back: Sprung weight is everything the springs carry, including the body, frame, engine, transmission, and passengers. It is separate from unsprung weight, which moves with the wheel instead of resting on the springs.

front: What is unsprung weight, and why does lowering it improve ride quality?
back: Unsprung weight is everything that moves with the wheel, including the wheel and tire, brake rotor and caliper, hub, and roughly half the weight of the springs, control arms, and axle shafts. Lower unsprung weight lets the wheel follow the road more easily because the spring and shock have less mass to control.

front: What is jounce and what limits it?
back: Jounce (compression) is upward wheel travel toward the body, as when a tire hits a bump. Maximum compression is limited by a jounce bumper, also called a bump stop, so the suspension never bottoms metal to metal.

front: What is rebound and what limits it?
back: Rebound (extension) is downward wheel travel away from the body as the spring pushes the wheel back after a bump. Rebound travel is limited by the shock absorber or strut rather than by a separate bumper.

front: Why does the exam test camber and toe changes during jounce for specific suspension designs?
back: Different suspension geometries move the wheel through different arcs as it travels up and down, so camber and toe do not stay constant on every design. Knowing which designs change these angles during jounce, such as twin I-beam or semi-trailing arm, helps predict wear patterns and diagnose complaints.

front: What does radial tire construction mean?
back: The body ply cords run at 90 degrees to the direction of travel, straight across from bead to bead. This lets the sidewall flex independently of the tread. That keeps a larger, more stable contact patch on the road than a bias ply tire.

front: What is the tire bead and what does it do?
back: The bead is a bundle of high tensile steel wires wrapped in rubber. It anchors the tire to the rim. It also resists the force of inflation pressure trying to push the tire off the wheel.

front: What job do the belts do inside a tire?
back: Belts are normally two layers of steel cord running around the circumference under the tread. They stabilize the tread and resist punctures. They also hold the tread flat against the road.

front: In the size P225/60R16 97T, what does the 60 mean?
back: The 60 is the aspect ratio. It means the sidewall height is 60 percent of the section width. For a 225 mm section width that sidewall stands about 135 mm tall.

front: In P225/60R16 97T, what does the 97 tell you?
back: The 97 is the load index, a code number tied to a maximum load per tire. In this case it corresponds to 730 kg at the tire's maximum rated pressure. A higher load index means the tire can carry more weight.

front: How do you read a tire's speed rating letter?
back: The speed rating letter is the maximum sustained speed the tire is built for. Common ratings climb through S, T, H, V, and W as speed capability increases. A replacement tire should meet or exceed the vehicle manufacturer's original speed rating.

front: What is different about LT tire sizing compared to P-metric?
back: LT tires carry a load range letter such as C, D, or E that reflects ply strength and maximum inflation pressure. They often list two load capacities, one for single wheel use and a lower one for dual wheel use. A P-metric tire used in light truck service must have its load capacity derated by dividing by 1.10.

front: How do you read a tire's DOT date code, for example 3223?
back: The last four digits of the DOT code are the date code. The first two digits are the week of manufacture and the last two are the year. A code of 3223 means the tire was built in the 32nd week of 2023.

front: What does a UTQG treadwear grade of 500 actually compare?
back: Treadwear is a number comparing wear life to a reference tire rated 100 under controlled test conditions. A 500 rated tire should last about five times as long as that reference tire. The number is only fair to compare within one manufacturer's own tire line.

front: What does the UTQG traction grade actually measure?
back: Traction is graded AA, A, B, or C. It measures straight line wet braking performance only. It does not measure cornering grip at all.

front: What is the difference between the mountain snowflake symbol and the M+S marking?
back: The peaked mountain and snowflake symbol means the tire passed a tested snow traction performance standard. The older M+S marking is only a mud and snow tread pattern claim with no performance test behind it. In Canada, insurance discounts and Quebec's winter tire law recognize the mountain snowflake symbol, not plain M+S.

front: Where should you get the correct tire inflation pressure from?
back: Use the tire placard, normally found on the driver's door jamb. The sidewall figure is only the maximum pressure the tire can hold, not the recommended setting. Setting every tire to the sidewall maximum is a classic mistake.

front: Why should tire pressure be checked cold?
back: Cold means the vehicle has sat about three hours or been driven less than roughly 2 km. Driving heats the air inside the tire and raises the pressure reading. Bleeding a hot tire down to the cold spec leaves it underinflated once it cools.

front: What tread wear pattern points to overinflation?
back: Overinflation shrinks the contact patch so the tire rides mainly on the tread center. This causes wear concentrated across the center of the tread only. The shoulders stay relatively unworn compared to the middle.

front: What tread wear pattern points to underinflation?
back: Underinflation lets the sidewalls flex excessively and pushes more load onto the outer parts of the tread. This causes wear on both shoulders with a good center. It also builds heat and raises rolling resistance.

front: What causes one-shoulder-only tire wear?
back: One shoulder wearing more than the other points to a camber problem. Excessive negative camber wears the inside shoulder, and excessive positive camber wears the outside shoulder. A sagging spring that changed the camber angle can cause the same pattern.

front: What causes feathered (saw tooth) tire wear?
back: Feathering is caused by incorrect toe. The tire scrubs sideways slightly with every meter it rolls, wearing each rib to a sharp edge on one side and a rounded edge on the other. Toe error is the fastest tread killer of all the alignment angles.

front: What causes cupped or scalloped tire wear?
back: Cupping shows as irregular dished patches around the tread circumference. It is caused by the tire bouncing rather than by steering geometry. Suspect worn shocks or struts, a loose wheel bearing, worn ball joints, or an out of balance wheel.

front: What tire rotation pattern is used for non-directional tires on a front wheel drive vehicle?
back: The common pattern is the forward cross. The rear tires cross to the opposite front corners, and the front tires move straight back. This evens out wear since the front tires carry, drive, and steer the car.

front: How must directional tires be rotated?
back: Directional tires are marked with a rotation arrow on the sidewall and must always keep turning the same direction. They can only rotate front to rear on the same side of the vehicle. They can only move to the other side if they are dismounted and remounted.

front: What makes a tire puncture repairable under trade standards?
back: A puncture is repairable only if it lies in the crown, the tread area between the outer circumferential grooves. It must also be no larger than 6 mm (1/4 inch). Any injury to the shoulder or sidewall makes the tire non-repairable.

front: What is the only accepted method for repairing a tire puncture?
back: The only accepted repair is a combination plug and patch, or a one piece plug-patch unit. It must be installed from inside the tire after the tire is dismounted and inspected. A string plug pushed in from outside, a patch alone, or aerosol sealant do not meet trade standards.

front: What is the maximum pressure allowed when seating tire beads during mounting?
back: Never exceed 275 kPa (40 psi) when seating beads. If the beads have not seated by then, deflate the tire, relubricate the beads, reposition the tire, and try again. Exceeding this pressure risks a dangerous bead blowout.

front: What is the difference between static and dynamic wheel imbalance?
back: Static imbalance means the assembly is heavier at one point around its circumference, and it causes wheel tramp, a vertical hopping. Dynamic imbalance means weight is unevenly distributed side to side across the assembly width, causing shimmy, a side to side wobble felt in the steering wheel. Dynamic imbalance needs weights on both the inner and outer rim planes to correct.

front: What does road force balancing measure that ordinary spin balancing does not?
back: A road force balancer presses a load roller against the spinning tire to measure stiffness variation and loaded runout, called road force. A tire can be perfectly balanced yet still vibrate due to a stiff spot or excessive runout. The machine can direct match mounting to cancel much of the assembly runout.

front: What is the difference between radial and lateral tire runout?
back: Radial runout is the up and down variation, measured on the center tread rib or the bead seat area of the wheel. Lateral runout is the side to side wobble, measured on the sidewall or the vertical face of the rim. Typical service limits are about 1.5 mm for an assembled tire and wheel.

front: What speed range and vibration pattern points to tire and wheel imbalance or runout?
back: A vibration felt from about 80 to 120 km/h that changes with road speed, not engine speed, points to tire and wheel imbalance or runout. This differs from an acceleration-only vibration, which points to driveline angles or a worn joint. Always road test, then spin balance, then check runout before selling parts.

front: What is the difference between direct and indirect TPMS?
back: Direct TPMS uses a battery powered sensor inside each wheel that transmits actual measured pressure and temperature by radio. Indirect TPMS has no pressure sensors and instead uses ABS wheel speed sensors to detect a smaller rolling radius on an underinflated tire. Indirect systems cost less but cannot display actual pressures and can miss all four tires being equally low.

front: What should be replaced whenever a direct TPMS tire is dismounted?
back: The sensor's serviceable parts should be replaced with a service kit: the valve core, sealing grommet, nut, and cap. The nickel plated valve core must never be swapped for a standard brass core, since brass corrodes against the aluminum stem. The small sensor nut must be torqued to specification because it strips easily.

front: What is the difference between positive and negative wheel offset?
back: Positive offset means the mounting face sits outboard of the rim's centerline, tucking the wheel in toward the vehicle. Negative offset pushes the wheel and tire outboard, producing a deep dish look. Changing offset changes the scrub radius and the loads placed on wheel bearings and steering parts.

front: What is the difference between hub-centric and lug-centric wheels?
back: Hub-centric wheels are located by a machined centre bore that fits closely over the hub's pilot flange, so the hub centres the wheel. Lug-centric wheels are centred instead by the tapered seats of the lug nuts and must be tightened progressively with the wheel off the ground. Aftermarket wheels with oversized centre bores often need hub-centric rings to avoid vibration.

front: Why should you avoid oiling wheel studs before torquing lug nuts?
back: Lubricated threads produce far more actual clamping force at the same torque wrench reading than dry threads. This can overstretch and damage the studs. Studs should only be oiled if the manufacturer specifically calls for it.

front: How should lug nuts be tightened for final torque?
back: Snug the nuts in a star or crisscross pattern first, then lower the vehicle to the ground. Apply final torque with a calibrated torque wrench in the same star pattern, typically around 100 to 140 N.m on passenger vehicles. An impact gun alone routinely over torques, which stretches studs and can crack alloy wheels.

front: How do you adjust a serviceable tapered front wheel bearing?
back: Tighten the adjusting nut to a seating torque of roughly 20 to 30 N.m while rotating the wheel to seat the parts. Back the nut off, then retighten it finger tight or to the light value the maker specifies. Confirm end play of 0.025 to 0.13 mm with a dial indicator before installing a new cotter pin.

front: How do you check for play in a modern sealed wheel hub unit?
back: Raise the wheel and rock the tire at the 12 and 6 o'clock positions. To separate bearing play from steering linkage play, also rock at 3 and 9 o'clock or have a helper apply the brake pedal. Allowable play in a sealed hub is nearly zero, generally under about 0.05 mm.
